title: The portion, for life
hookLine: the weekly portion as a lifelong companion
tomorrow: a page of Talmud a day sounds heroic. what about half?

lines: WHEN IT ENDS, IT STARTS AGAIN.
cards: Some people rewatch the same comfort show every winter and swear it's different each time. The Torah reading works like that, on purpose.
Week by week, a portion at a time, the whole Torah is read aloud, and when it ends, it starts again. So is it a rerun? And how fast should you go around?
Inside the tradition there are two real answers, and both are old.

teach.h: ONE YEAR: EVERYONE ON ONE PAGE.
teach.b: The first view: one year. A portion every week, the whole Torah, and around again. Its case is togetherness.

Wherever you go, it's the same portion that week, so a guest at any table can talk about this week's Torah. And on Simchat Torah, the last words of Deuteronomy are read and Genesis begins right after, the same day.
No gap. The second view: slower.
The Talmud mentions people in the land of Israel who finished the Torah in three years, and some communities read that way now, about a third of each portion. Its case is depth.
Time to sit with a story long enough for it to stay. Notice what the two views share. Nobody reads the Torah once and shelves it.

teach.h: TWICE THE TEXT, ONCE THE TRANSLATION.
teach.b: The Talmud even asks each person to complete the portions along with the community, reading the text twice and the translation once. You come around again, either way.
And you're not the reader you were last year, which is why it isn't a rerun.
Something to tell a friend tonight: in synagogue, the end of the Torah and its beginning are read on the same day.

how: Synagogues read the Torah in weekly portions; some finish it in a year and begin again on Simchat Torah, and some follow a three-year cycle. Some learners also read the week's portion at home.

games.q: your friend's synagogue reads about a third of each portion, over three years. you grew up with the whole portion every week. what's her side's best case?
o: slower gives each story time to stay, and the Talmud knows a three-year cycle.
a third is easier, and the easier way is always the better one.
the yearly cycle is a newer invention, so hers is the only real one.
games.why: the three-year view argues for depth, and the Talmud mentions it. the one-year view argues for everyone on the same page. both come around again.

practice: If you know this week's portion, find its first verse and read it out loud. If not, read the first verse of the Torah: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."
Read it a second time, slower, and listen for one word that sounds different the second time around.

wordCard.voice: The portion: the parashah, the week's reading of the Torah, read in a cycle that ends and begins again.

orig.note: Hebrew: a portion; the week's Torah reading.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: the cycle never ends. Same words, a new reader, every time around. Bye for now.
